nature-acct-034.q: Which company ran a large advertising campaign that helped popularize the personal carbon footprint?

nature-acct-046.q: How do the internal and external water footprints differ?
nature-acct-046.a: The internal footprint uses domestic water; the external footprint is water used abroad to make imported goods.

nature-acct-063.q: What are the weaknesses of bottom-up LCA and of top-down EEIO?
nature-acct-063.a: Bottom-up LCA can assess specific products but suffers truncation, because no study can follow the whole supply chain; top-down EEIO multiplies greenhouse gas intensity by the final demand for each product.

nature-pol-050.q: What are examples of brownfield sites?
nature-pol-050.a: Abandoned factories, ash ponds, landfills, dry cleaners and gas stations.

nature-clim-234.q: How do damages grow with warming in the common base form of a climate damage function?
nature-clim-234.a: With the square of warming: 2 C causes 4 times and 3 C 9 times the damage of 1 C.

nature-pol-072.q: What does living near particle-emitting facilities do to people?
nature-pol-072.a: It raises PM2.5 exposure and rates of illness and death.

nature-pol-066.q: How does reuse differ from recycling?
nature-pol-066.a: Reuse does not break items down into raw materials, which saves time, money, energy and resources.

nature-pol-057.q: How many countries signed the 1992 Basel Convention, and what was it meant to stop?
nature-pol-057.a: 199 countries signed it to stop the flow of hazardous waste to poorer countries.

nature-pol-053.q: How does phytoremediation clean contaminated soil?
nature-pol-053.a: It uses deep-rooted plants to draw heavy metals out of the soil.

nature-pol-140.q: What led to the UK Clean Air Act 1956?
nature-pol-140.a: London's Great Smog of 1952; the Act set emission limits for households and businesses enforced by an inspectorate.

nature-pol-311.q: What is single-use development in urban sprawl?
nature-pol-311.a: It separates homes, work, shops and recreation so far that walking, transit and cycling are impractical and every activity needs a car.

nature-pol-173.q: What risk do government agencies face when regulating industries?
nature-pol-173.a: Regulatory capture by the industries they regulate.

nature-pol-160.q: Why did the Endangered Species Act become controversial?
nature-pol-160.a: Species could be listed without considering economic costs, so landowners and industries face lost opportunities and delays.

nature-pol-146.q: How is 'best available technology' read in practice?
nature-pol-146.a: Read literally it would demand the best technology regardless of cost, but in practice costs are also taken into account.

nature-pol-306.q: Why can sustainable aviation fuel decarbonize hard-to-abate flights?
nature-pol-306.a: As a drop-in replacement it needs no major aircraft engine changes, so it can decarbonize medium and long-haul flights.

nature-pol-143.q: How do cleanup laws differ from pollution-control laws?
nature-pol-143.a: They respond after the fact, so they must define both the needed response and who must carry it out or pay for it.

nature-pol-157.q: What did biodiversity banking grow out of?
nature-pol-157.a: US wetland mitigation banking and the 'no net loss' policies tied to the Act in the 1970s.

nature-pol-152.q: Which country announced the first tax on livestock carbon dioxide emissions?
nature-pol-152.a: Denmark, in June 2024, with the tax starting from 2030.

nature-pol-156.q: What are the four parts of water quality standards?
nature-pol-156.a: Designated uses, water quality criteria, an antidegradation policy and general policies.

nature-pol-165.q: What does a low-carbon fuel standard count that a tailpipe measure would miss?
nature-pol-165.a: It counts emissions over the fuel's whole life cycle, 'well to wheels', not just from the tailpipe.

nature-pol-081.q: How does a carbon tax differ from command-and-control rules?
nature-pol-081.a: Unlike rules that cap each polluter, a carbon tax lets market forces find the cheapest way to cut pollution.

nature-pol-124.q: Why are carbon taxes often regressive?
nature-pol-124.a: Taxes on everyday essentials such as food, fuel, energy and housing, including carbon taxes, are often regressive.

nature-pol-085.q: Which environmental taxes are the most common worldwide?
nature-pol-085.a: Energy taxes, levied on producing, distributing or using fuels such as coal, oil and gas.

nature-pol-089.q: What are the two dividends of the double dividend idea?
nature-pol-089.a: The first dividend is a cleaner environment; the second is a more efficient tax system from cutting distorting taxes such as income tax.

nature-pol-130.q: How do fuel taxes that fund highways act as user fees?
nature-pol-130.a: Those who drive more pay more for roads.

nature-pol-253.q: What must polluters do under cap and trade?
nature-pol-253.a: Hold permits equal to their emissions; one that wants to emit more must buy permits from others willing to sell.

nature-pol-270.q: How did China respond after proposing a carbon tax in 2010?
nature-pol-270.a: It never passed the tax and set up an emissions trading scheme in February 2021 instead.

nature-pol-249.q: Why has carbon trading been called a form of colonialism?
nature-pol-249.a: It lets rich countries keep consuming while claiming savings abroad.

nature-pol-261.q: What is the main aim of the EU carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM)?
nature-pol-261.a: To stop carbon leakage by charging covered imports the same carbon price as EU producers pay under the EU ETS.

nature-pol-281.q: What monitoring did Acid Rain Program plants have to do?
nature-pol-281.a: They had to monitor SO2 and NOx continuously and send data to the EPA daily.

nature-pol-246.q: Why do free permits become windfall profits?
nature-pol-246.a: Firms that get free permits still raise prices to customers, so permits they did not need become windfall profits.

nature-pol-319.a: Non-monetary spillover effects on non-participants: a rendering plant's odours are negative, a neighbour's garden positive.

nature-pol-317.q: What did Paul Milgrom and Robert Wilson win the 2020 Nobel Memorial Prize for?
nature-pol-317.a: Advancing auction theory with new formats.

nature-pol-184.q: What do certification and traceability do under sustainability standards?
nature-pol-184.a: Certification checks that a business meets the standard, and traceability follows certified goods along the supply chain, often ending in a label for shoppers.

nature-pol-218.a: The logo, used by most certification services, that certified products can carry.

nature-pol-206.q: How do production and consumption subsidies differ?
nature-pol-206.a: Production subsidies help suppliers expand output by offsetting costs; consumption subsidies lower the price consumers pay.

nature-pol-196.q: Why is extended producer responsibility cited as a tool against planned obsolescence?
nature-pol-196.a: Making producers pay for recycling may lead them to design less toxic, longer-lasting electronics.

nature-pol-215.q: How far did the farmland bird population fall between 1980 and 2009?
nature-pol-215.a: From 600 million to 300 million, a loss of 50%.

nature-pol-315.q: How does UNESCO define the right to know?
nature-pol-315.a: It lets people take part in decisions that affect them in an informed way while holding governments and others accountable.
